title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
statement: You get the first nodes of two singly linked lists. Both are sorted from small to large. Join them into one sorted list by relinking the existing nodes, and return its first node. Either list may be empty.

example.caption: Two sorted lists become one. Equal values keep their order, list1 first.

idea.sentence: Start the answer with a fake node, then keep linking the smaller front node of the two lists after the last node you linked.

jargon.plain: A throwaway node placed before the real list. It gives tail something to point at on the very first pick.
A pointer to the last node of the merged list so far. New nodes are linked after it.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: the two sorted lists, e.g. [1,2,4], [1,3,4]

compare.bruteLabel: Collect all values, sort them, build a new list

rows.name: Collect and sort
rows.note: Ignores that both lists are already sorted and allocates new nodes.

rows.name: Dummy head and tail
rows.note: Each node is linked once. The only extra node is the dummy.

fast.takeaway: Both inputs are sorted, so the smallest remaining value is always one of two fronts. One pass is enough.

stages.title: Fake head and tail
stages.note: Create a throwaway node. tail starts on it. The answer will be whatever hangs after it.

stages.title: Pick the smaller front
stages.note: Compare the two front nodes. Take the smaller one (list1 on a tie) and link it after tail.

stages.title: Move tail
stages.note: tail steps onto the node we just linked, ready for the next pick.

stages.title: Attach the rest
stages.note: When one list is empty, the other is already sorted. Link it on whole.

stages.title: Return dummy.next
stages.note: Skip the fake node. Its next is the real first node.

edges.title: Both empty
edges.why: The loop never runs. dummy.next is still null, which is the right empty answer.

edges.title: One empty
edges.why: The loop is skipped and the leftover list is attached whole.

edges.title: Equal values
edges.why: On a tie take list1. Either order gives the same values, but a fixed rule keeps it predictable.

edges.title: One list far shorter
edges.why: list1 runs out early. The long tail of list2 is attached in one step, not copied.

gotchas.text: Return dummy.next, not dummy. The dummy is only scaffolding.
Do not forget the leftover. When the loop stops, one list can still have nodes. Link it after tail.
tail.next has the type ListNode | null, so tail = tail.next will not type-check. Keep the chosen node in a variable (pick) and assign tail = pick.
Write dummy := &ListNode{} and tail := dummy. If you wrote dummy := ListNode{} then tail := dummy, tail would be a copy and the answer would be lost.
Go has no ternary and no ??. Use an if / else for the leftover, and compare against nil, not 0.

recap.key: A fake first node means every pick is the same line: tail.next = smaller. Return dummy.next.
moves: While both lists have nodes, link the smaller front after tail
Move tail onto it, then advance that list
Attach the leftover list. Return dummy.next
